615.bp: When you predict weather, electricity demand, or stock prices hours or days ahead, small errors snowball—today's mistake poisons tomorrow's guess. The real goal is to give decision-makers at scale (electricity grids, supply chains, trading floors) accurate enough forecasts to act on, even when the future is choppy and data is noisy.
615.wh: Transformer models, which have worked brilliantly for language, stumble here because they chain predictions together (each step feeds the next), so one mistake cascades. They also fall apart when the test data doesn't match the training data—imagine a model trained on mild weather trying to predict a hurricane.
615.ap: The authors build a leaner Transformer and pair it with a new optimizer called Escape-Explore. The optimizer has two jobs: when training gets stuck (imagine rolling a ball in a valley, trapped between two walls), it first escapes the trap, then explores outward to find better ground—avoiding dead-ends that trap ordinary optimizers.
615.ww: Escaping traps helps the model learn richer patterns rather than settling for mediocre shortcuts. Exploring widely makes the final solution more stable and generalizable—when test data differs from training, a solution found on high ground is less fragile than one wedged in a narrow crevice.
615.po: On real web data (11 time-series benchmarks plus medical imaging), this method matches the best existing models but with better stability and generalization—crucially, it works across both forecasting and vision tasks, not just one.

616.bp: The world is constantly changing—a political situation evolves, companies merge, facts shift. We want machines to keep a memory of how things connect (Entity A relates to Entity B via relationship C) and fill in missing links when data is incomplete, so we understand what's likely to happen next.
616.wh: Most methods focus on order (what happened first, second, third) or raw structure (who's connected to whom), but they ignore the semantic meaning—the difference between 'political event' and 'economic crisis,' even though both are changes. Without semantic depth, the model misses subtle patterns.
616.ap: This method uses large language models to label entities and relationships with semantic tags (like 'political event,' 'economic activity'). It then builds two graphs—one capturing relations between entities, another between the semantic labels—and runs convolution operations (neighborhood aggregation) on both, letting information flow from labels into entity predictions.
616.ww: Semantic tags act like interpretable clues: they help the model understand that a 'political event' entity should behave differently from an 'economic activity' one. Higher-order interactions (many-to-many relationships) let distant but thematically similar facts reinforce each other.
616.po: On standard knowledge graph benchmarks, this dual-graph approach completes missing links more accurately than single-graph methods, especially in complex, evolving scenarios where semantic distinctions matter.

617.bp: Modern search engines face a new problem: instead of returning a ranked list of links, they now generate document IDs directly (like 'doc_4829_Q1'). The advantage is crisp and fast, but the reality is harsh—whenever new documents arrive (new blog posts, products, papers), the model must learn them immediately without retraining.
617.wh: Retraining from scratch is slow and expensive (days of GPU time). Incremental training (adding new data without retraining) causes catastrophic forgetting—the model unlearns old documents while learning new ones. Also, the decoder (the part mapping thought patterns to document IDs) struggles because many different queries might retrieve overlapping sets of IDs, so it's hard to tell them apart.
617.ap: Instead of retraining, the authors use surgical model editing: identify which neural network layers control document ID mapping, tweak their weights carefully, and inject smart labels (soft labels that preserve query-specific nuances) to make the edits learn which ID goes with which query.
617.ww: Surgical edits are faster than retraining and avoid catastrophic forgetting because they only touch the relevant wiring. Soft labels preserve the query context, so the model doesn't confuse similar IDs even when they overlap.
617.po: The method adapts to new documents without full retraining, achieving performance near incremental training but in far less time, making generative retrieval practical for live, continuously-updated document collections.

618.bp: When researchers publish code, they write README files explaining datasets, scripts, and third-party libraries. These free-form documents hold practical knowledge that's locked away in unstructured text—if we could extract and link this metadata automatically, research would be more discoverable and reproducible.
618.wh: README files use Markdown (a loose format with little structure) and mix casual language with technical detail. Existing information extraction datasets focus on academic papers, not implementation details. The gap means we lack training data to teach machines what 'dataset,' 'license,' or 'requirement' looks like in a README.
618.ap: The authors manually labeled 200 README files, marking 10,000+ text spans with 10 entity types (like 'Dataset,' 'Framework,' 'License'). They tested two approaches: large language models (given a README, guess the entities) and fine-tuned Transformers (Transformers trained on the labeled examples).
618.ww: Manual annotation creates ground truth—a reliable standard to measure against. The comparison between LLMs and fine-tuned models reveals that implementation-level entities behave differently from paper-level ones, so a model trained on papers alone will fail on code.
618.po: The labeled dataset and baselines now let researchers train entity extractors specific to README files. A downstream experiment shows these extracted entities support artifact discovery (finding related code and datasets), validating the practical value.

619.bp: Traffic forecasts power smart traffic lights, route recommendations, and congestion alerts—decisions made every minute across cities. Accurate predictions prevent gridlock and guide thousands of drivers. The challenge is that traffic is deeply spatial (neighbors affect each other) and temporal (patterns repeat hourly, daily, seasonally).
619.wh: Most graph methods only capture pairwise links ('Road A connects to Road B'). But traffic is richer: groups of roads interact together, time patterns interweave with geography, and daily/seasonal rhythms matter. Miss these higher-order interactions and your predictions become fragile.
619.ap: The method builds two hypergraphs (graphs where edges can connect many nodes at once, not just pairs). One captures spatial proximity (geographical neighborhoods), the other temporal patterns (which traffic series behave similarly, detected by mutual information). Both feed through a convolution network that learns node representations, followed by a GRU-MLP module that captures both local dynamics and global trends. Periodic features (daily, weekly patterns extracted via Fourier transform) add semantic richness.
619.ww: Hyperedges (many-to-many connections) naturally express 'this cluster of roads moves together.' Mutual information in the temporal graph finds nonlinear patterns (erratic but correlated flows) that linear methods miss. Periodic features give the model a calendar sense.
619.po: On real traffic networks, this method forecasts flow more accurately than single-graph baselines, especially during complex rush-hour periods where spatial and temporal interactions are most tangled.

620.bp: Imagine a surveillance camera needs to track the same car across different angles and times. Vehicle re-identification answers: 'Is this the same car?'—crucial for parking lots, toll plazas, and stolen-vehicle alerts. The catch is that the same car looks different from different angles and under occlusion.
620.wh: Features get tangled: the model learns identity (it's Car #47) but also captures angle ('from the left side'), lighting, and occlusion patterns. These extra features muddy the waters—a car seen from the front looks so different from the rear that the model struggles to match them.
620.ap: The method uses two mechanisms to disentangle features. First, multi-head attention separates which parts of the image matter for identity (tire pattern, color distribution) versus which are pose artifacts (angle, lighting). Second, region-aware sparse attention and symmetry-aware attention focus on the most stable, identity-defining features while suppressing redundant noise.
620.ww: Disentangling isolates the signal (identity) from the noise (viewpoint, occlusion). By separately handling symmetric features (both sides of a car) and asymmetric ones (unique scratches, damage), the model learns finer distinctions that survive viewpoint changes.
620.po: On standard vehicle datasets (VeRi776, VehicleID), this method achieves better matching accuracy than existing approaches, especially in multi-view scenarios where cars are seen from many angles.

621.bp: Large language models now review contracts, screen job applications, and flag policy violations. If an adversary slips fraudulent information into the input, the model can make dangerous mistakes—approving a fake invoice, hiring a scammer, ignoring a threat. We need a defense that keeps the LLM honest.
621.wh: Standard defenses (adversarial training, input filtering) are brittle: they're not general (work on one fraud type but not others), hard to interpret (the user can't see why the model rejected something), and don't transfer well between different LLMs.
621.ap: This method builds a knowledge graph that maps suspicious phrases to fraud tactics (e.g., 'urgent action required' maps to high-pressure manipulation). Given an input, it extracts keywords and fraud tactics, then augments the prompt sent to the LLM with highlighted keywords and explanatory evidence—essentially saying 'hey, this smells like tactic X, be careful.'
621.ww: Knowledge graphs are interpretable (you can see the fraud tactic connections) and general (the same tactics appear across fraud types). Augmenting the prompt with structured evidence guides the LLM toward defensive reasoning without requiring model retraining.
621.po: Across four popular LLMs and five fraud types (contract manipulation, job scams, policy violations, etc.), this defense outperforms prior methods, offering both better robustness and explainable traces of why the model was suspicious.

622.bp: Autonomous AI agents—systems that make decisions and take actions over time with minimal human oversight—are moving into banks, hospitals, and power grids. A rogue agent could embezzle money, alter medical records, or sabotage infrastructure. We need to rethink what 'insider threat' means when the insider is not human but machine.
622.wh: Insider threat detection was designed for humans: monitor login times, file access, email patterns. But an AI agent has no 9-to-5 schedule, doesn't sleep, and can be reprogrammed instantly. Traditional behavior baselines don't apply, and humans have a hard time spotting when an agent's goals have drifted.
622.ap: This is a position paper (not a concrete tool, but a manifesto). It argues that we need new categories: agent role drift (gradual expansion of an agent's decision scope), manipulation (other agents tricking it), and emergent misuse (unintended consequences of its learning). It sketches research directions: better agent observability (can we see agent reasoning?), auditability (can we replay and explain actions?), and memory isolation (preventing agents from colluding).
622.ww: An AI system's misbehavior often has a root cause (bad objective function, poisoned training data, interaction with another agent) that's invisible to current tools. Making agents transparent and auditable is the only way to catch insider threats before they cause damage.
622.po: The paper identifies key gaps in current security practice and proposes an agenda for governance, monitoring, and detection mechanisms specifically designed for autonomous systems—setting the stage for safer multi-agent deployments.

623.bp: Graph neural networks power recommendation systems, fraud detection, and social networks—they learn representations by aggregating neighbor information. But what if an attacker poisons the training graph, injecting fake edges or nodes? The model learns to misclassify specific target nodes, like a sleeper cell in a recommendation system.
623.wh: Existing defenses look for anomalies by comparing poisoned nodes to clean ones. But clever attackers design triggers (injected edges or features) that blend in, indistinguishable from normal nodes. Detecting anomalies becomes impossible if the attacker mimics benign behavior.
623.ap: This method identifies specific neural dimensions (embedding coordinates) that activate more often in poisoned models—'backdoor neurons.' The authors then reverse-engineer which graph triggers activate those neurons, unlearn the poisoned knowledge at that neuron level, and recover the model's clean behavior.
623.ww: Backdoor neurons are a structural vulnerability: information in the graph flows through the network in predictable ways, so poisoning concentrates damage in a few dimensions. By surgically targeting those dimensions rather than trying to detect triggers, the defense bypasses the attacker's camouflage.
623.po: On multiple graph datasets, this neuron-level defense removes backdoor effects more reliably than detection-based approaches, restoring clean predictions without retraining from scratch.

624.bp: Streaming recommendation systems (Netflix, YouTube, Amazon) face a hard reality: most users interact sparsely (they watch a few videos), most items get little exposure (99% of videos are never clicked), and new content arrives constantly. These long-tail distributions confound most algorithms, which do well for popular items but fail for obscure ones.
624.wh: Collaborative sparsity (few interactions for tail users/items) means the model has less signal. Existing LLM-based methods only embed items as single vectors, missing semantic relationships ('westerns' and 'noir films' are similar). Head-tail tradeoffs are unavoidable: improve tail recommendations, and head accuracy often drops.
624.ap: This method uses LLMs to build global semantic understanding of items. For tail items, it creates a fuzzy prototype that lets them borrow features from semantically related head items (a rare western inherits viewing patterns from popular westerns). For sparse users, it aligns and distills across similar users. Lightweight regularization balances semantic and collaborative signals globally.
624.ww: Semantic alignment shares knowledge across the taxonomy—tail items and users are no longer alone but anchored to semantic neighbors with richer signal. Global regularization prevents the model from gaming head accuracy to boost tail performance.
624.po: Across three datasets and multiple backbones, this method improves tail recommendations while maintaining or slightly improving head accuracy—solving the long-standing head-tail seesaw problem.

625.bp: Graphs are not static—friendships form and dissolve, markets rise and fall, networks evolve. Graph neural networks trained on one era's data often fail on the next because the distribution has shifted. Real-world graph changes (link formation patterns, node behavior) are driven by underlying environments that change over time.
625.wh: Dynamic graph networks use temporal message-passing (propagating information through time), but environment shifts confuse the model: factors that mattered yesterday might not matter today. The model overfits to training environments and fails to generalize.
625.ap: The method models multiple possible environment shifts (using variational inference to extract pseudo-environments from the data), then trains a mixture of experts—different subnetworks, each specialized for one environment. An alignment objective forces all experts to agree on invariant (stable) representations, filtering out environment-specific noise.
625.ww: By explicitly modeling environment variation, the network avoids mistaking temporary correlations for true patterns. The mixture-of-experts structure lets the model adapt which expert to trust as conditions shift, while the alignment objective ensures robustness.
625.po: On real and synthetic dynamic graphs, this approach significantly outperforms models trained without environment awareness, especially when test data drift away from training conditions.

626.bp: Web services face advanced attacks buried in system logs—adversaries hide intrusions by changing file access patterns, forging process relationships, and reordering activities. Provenance-based detection reconstructs these causal chains to spot inconsistencies. The challenge: attackers can subtly manipulate the graph to evade detection.
626.wh: Graph-based detectors are vulnerable to graph manipulation attacks: adversaries tweak the structure just enough to fool the model without creating obvious anomalies. Applying arbitrary perturbations (noise) for robustness destroys the causal logic that made provenance useful in the first place.
626.ap: This method generates robust representations using logic-aware augmentation: instead of random noise, it injects semantically valid perturbations that preserve the causal meaning of provenance graphs. It then uses contrastive learning—training the model to recognize similar behaviors even under logical transformations while distinguishing adversarial perturbations.
626.ww: Logic-aware perturbations maintain causal semantics, so the model learns representations grounded in what attacks actually look like, not statistical artifacts. Contrastive learning is inherently robust: by learning invariances to benign transformations, the model becomes insensitive to harmless graph variations.
626.po: On multiple provenance datasets, this framework outperforms state-of-the-art anomaly detectors in resisting graph manipulation while maintaining high detection accuracy and computational efficiency.

627.bp: Web3 (blockchain, DeFi, NFTs) needs identity systems where users control their own data without a central authority. Decentralized identity lets someone prove 'I'm member of this gaming community' without revealing their real name or linking it to their DeFi wallet. The challenge: across multiple independent blockchains and services, maintaining privacy while staying traceable for bad actors.
627.wh: Existing decentralized identity systems use a central committee to manage identity, creating a bottleneck: as the system grows, the committee becomes a target. Cross-domain privacy is impossible when users frequently move between services (DeFi → Gaming → DAO) because movement patterns expose identity.
627.ap: This system uses sharding to partition the identity infrastructure across independent domain committees, scaling horizontally. It introduces a domain-hiding presentation protocol based on ring signatures (a cryptographic trick where a user proves membership in a trusted set without revealing which one). Users can present themselves to different services without linking their activities.
627.ww: Sharding eliminates the bottleneck: each domain committee handles only its users, not the whole world. Ring signatures hide which trusted domain the user came from, so even if someone interacts across many services, the connections remain hidden.
627.po: The system achieves strong cross-domain anonymity (interactions in DeFi don't leak to Gaming), efficient traceability (when a user breaks rules, authorities can identify them), and scalability comparable to non-privacy systems.

628.bp: On Twitter, Reddit, and news sites, events unfold in real time—a product launch, a political scandal, a natural disaster. Machines can cluster the flood of messages into coherent narratives, alerting users and journalists to emerging stories. The challenge is capturing how social information spreads in waves, with messages reinforcing and interfering with each other.
628.wh: Standard graph convolution networks assume information diffuses in a single, smooth wave—each node gets updated once, like heat spreading through a room. Real social diffusion is messier: a breaking story gets shared, dies down, then resurges when new evidence emerges. Messages interact—some reinforce (retweets agreeing), others clash (dispute threads).
628.ap: The method models information diffusion using wave physics. A spectral filter (the Helmholtz equation from acoustics/electromagnetism) captures oscillatory wave propagation. A physical interaction force adjusts connection strengths: messages in the same event attract each other, while messages across events repel. Text encoding and timestamps add context.
628.ww: Wave-based propagation naturally captures oscillations and interference—when two social signals converge, they either amplify or cancel. Physical forces make the model attention-aware: it learns which connections matter for which events, adapting the graph structure dynamically.
628.po: On real social event detection benchmarks, this physics-inspired approach outperforms standard GCN-based methods, especially at disentangling overlapping stories and tracking multi-wave diffusion patterns.

629.bp: Technology-Assisted Review (TAR) systems help teams find relevant documents in massive collections—used in legal discovery (finding responsive documents in millions of files), systematic literature review (screening papers for meta-analysis), and now for large-scale Web content moderation and information access. The challenge: ensuring fairness, transparency, and trustworthiness at Web scale.
629.wh: The Web is no longer just links to external pages—it's user-generated content, AI-generated syntheses, multilingual text, and constantly shifting. Existing TAR methods were built for static, well-organized collections. Applying them to Web data means dealing with heterogeneity, dynamic updates, and diverse languages, all while maintaining transparency and avoiding bias.
629.ap: This is a workshop proposal (not a research paper, but an agenda for the community). It brings together researchers from retrieval, Web science, AI governance, and law to discuss how TAR can be adapted for Web-scale challenges. Topics include intelligent retrieval (better ranking), human-in-the-loop learning (efficient feedback loops), explainability (why is this document relevant?), and integrating LLMs and knowledge graphs.
629.ww: Web-scale TAR is fundamentally about trustworthiness: if an automated system gates access to information, it must be auditable and fair. LLMs and knowledge graphs can enhance retrieval, but only if their reasoning is transparent. Human-in-the-loop keeps humans in control of high-stakes decisions.
629.po: The workshop aims to identify research gaps, foster collaboration, and chart directions for building TAR systems that work at Web scale while maintaining human oversight, fairness, and accountability in automated information access.
